B() { super(); show(); n += 100; }
@Override void show() { System.out.print(s + n + super.s + super.n + " "); }

lesson.title: Constructor and method, together
lesson.summary: B calls its superclass constructor, calls show(), then updates n.
steps: super() runs the superclass constructor. After it returns, B's field initializers and instance initializer blocks run, before the next statement, show().

show() is an instance-method call, so overriding matters. The shown implementation prints an expression using field names and super.field accesses. super selects superclass fields; the bare names may be inherited or declared in B.
n += 100 happens after the call. For a numeric n, this adds 100 to its existing value; it does not simply set it to 100.
lesson.note: A call made inside the superclass constructor could run an override earlier, before subclass initialization. Also, + can add numbers before it starts joining text; it inserts no spaces of its own.

output.explanation: Exact values and output need the field types, initializers and superclass constructor. Missing declarations do not mean zero or null.

concepts.explanation: An explicit call to the superclass constructor as part of constructing this same object. It is the call that starts superclass construction, not a second call after that construction has already finished.
Asks the compiler to check that this method overrides or implements an eligible method. The annotation does not cause runtime dispatch.

lesson.title: Explanation
lesson.summary: Demonstrates how field initialization order and type-based access rules interact during object construction.
lesson.note: Fields and static methods use the declared reference type, while instance methods use the actual object's class. That is why x.s gives A's field but x.show() calls B's method.
steps: new B() runs: A's fields initialize (s="A", n=1), then A's constructor calls show(). Because the object is really a B, B's show() runs, but B's fields haven't been set yet, so s is null and n is 0. It prints "null0A1 ".
A's constructor finishes: n becomes 1+10=11. Control returns to B, where B's fields initialize in source order: s="B", n=2, then the instance block makes n=2*3=6.
B's constructor body runs: show() prints "B6A11 ", then n becomes 6+100=106.
x.show() dispatches to B's show() at runtime, printing "B106A11 ".

The println line: x.s and x.n use A's fields ("A", 11) because x's declared type is A. The casts to B give B's fields ("B", 106). x.who() is static so it uses the declared type A, returning "a". ((A) null).who() also returns "a" because it is static and doesn't touch the null reference.

concepts.explanation: A class declared static inside another class. It does not need an instance of the enclosing class. It is nested, but is not a non-static inner class.
For instance methods, Java picks the version from the object's actual class at runtime. For fields and static methods, it uses the declared type of the reference.

lesson.title: Explanation
lesson.summary: Joins a list of names into a single comma-separated string and prints it.
steps: Create a list called `names` holding two strings: "Ada" and "Lin".
Call `", ".join(names)` — this glues the list items together using ", " as the separator, producing one single string: "Ada, Lin".
`print` displays that string on the screen.

concepts.explanation: An ordered collection of items. Counting the items is different from adding their values.
A method that connects all items in a list into one string, using the string you give it as the glue between items.
